head:
Adults · Physical activity

France compared with the world: where do we really stand?

You often read country rankings: this country moves little, that one a lot, and France sits somewhere in the middle. Before asking where you stand, you need to know whether those rankings hold up. This article follows a single question, from the broadest level to the most precise: what can actually be compared between countries, and what can be said about France when we stick to what is comparable?

The problem

A country ranking gives the impression of a measurement. A table with aligned percentages, ranks, one country at the top, one at the bottom. You remember one sentence: “France does better than Germany”, or “Indians are more sedentary than Americans”. Yet these sentences rest on choices the table does not show: which year, which study, which definition of “active”, and above all how anyone knew what people were doing.

The major international studies on the subject do not measure your body. They ask adults what they say they do, then convert the answers to a common definition: fewer than 150 minutes of moderate activity per week, or fewer than 75 minutes of vigorous activity, or the equivalent, is what the WHO calls “insufficient” activity.1,2 This definition is useful, but it is applied to answers, not to measurements.

So there are two levels that should not be confused. The first is an observation: to what extent do French adults report being active, compared with adults in other countries? The second is a question of method: are these comparisons made on common bases, and which ones are? If they are not, a rank has no meaning, and it is better to know that before reassuring or worrying yourself.

The question

Where does France stand relative to other countries for adult physical activity, and what can honestly be compared from one country to another?

We proceed in six steps: how a country gets a figure, why the same country can have two, what is comparable between regions, what changes when a different question is asked, what proxy indicators and self-report are worth, and then what can be said about France itself. The answer comes after that.

What is at stake

The first stake is not getting the diagnosis wrong. If you believe your country is “average” when that ranking mixes years and methods, you may ease off an effort that was not one, or on the contrary blame yourself for a gap that does not exist. The second is a public decision stake: a government that reads that it is “behind” or “ahead” will not choose the same actions, and the global target of a 15% relative reduction in inactivity by 2030 is judged on these figures.1,2

The third is personal. Insufficient activity is a risk factor for non-communicable diseases, and it is associated with poorer physical, cognitive and mental health, according to the summary of the largest recent study.1 This is not an abstract statistical subject: what you do in an ordinary week weighs on your level of fitness, which you can measure.

Finally, there is a stake of trust in the figures. A web page that shows percentages by country and presents them as comparable commits its author. If one of the figures comes from a 2016 study and another from a 2022 estimate, the reader is misled, even if each figure taken alone is accurate. That is the reason for this article: each number that follows says where it comes from, what it measures, and what it can or cannot be set against.
rest:
Step 1 of 6 · The whole world

How a country gets a figure, and why the gaps shown are huge

Let us start with the widest picture, that of the rankings. A large 2018 analysis, which pooled 358 population surveys and 1.9 million participants, produced country figures for 2016.4 Picked up by the press and encyclopaedias, it gives values that stand out: Kuwait 67%, Brazil 47%, United States 40%, United Kingdom 35.9%, India 34%, China 14.1%, Uganda 5.5%.5,6

In the same 2016 study, the gap between countries runs from 5.5% to 67%

Adults with insufficient physical activity, 2016, self-reported. A selection of countries, not a full ranking. Values from the study by Guthold et al. (Lancet Global Health, 2018), read in two secondary sources, not in the article itself.5,6

What this means

Kuwait is more than twelve times the level of Uganda (67 divided by 5.5, derived calculation). No health gap that wide is plausible between two adult populations: part of the difference comes from what is reported and from what is counted as activity. The most common explanation is that in countries where work is physical, walking and carrying count as activity, whereas in countries where people work seated, only leisure counts. This explanation is not demonstrated by the pages read: it is a hypothesis. What is established is that a country’s figure depends on how people are asked.

How are these figures produced? Not every country has its own survey, and those that exist do not all use the same questionnaire. The Indian national survey, for example, uses the GPAQ questionnaire, the WHO’s own.3 In France, the Esteban survey used a different questionnaire, the RPAQ, which covers the previous four weeks.13,14 Where data are missing, a statistical model fills the gaps: the 2024 study has surveys for 163 countries and territories, and publishes estimates for 197, that is 34 without a survey of their own (derived calculation).1

A country figure is therefore neither a direct measurement nor a single snapshot. It is a constructed estimate, and its reliability depends on a chain of choices. It remains to see whether, at least, two estimates for the same country agree.

Step 2 of 6 · A single country

The same country can have two figures, depending on the year of publication

The second step is the most baffling, because it concerns a single country. Take India, one of the most cited. The WHO’s 2024 factsheet for India gives an annual series of adults with insufficient activity: 22.3% in 2000, 27.7% in 2005, 33.7% in 2010, 40.1% in 2015, 46.8% in 2020 and 49.4% in 2022.3

India has two figures for the same period, depending on the study that publishes them

Curve: WHO 2024 database, adults aged 18 and over, age-standardised (WHO India factsheet).3 Circled point: 2016 estimate from the 2018 study, read in a secondary source.5 The two do not refer to exactly the same year: 2015 on one side, 2016 on the other.

What this means

The 2018 study gave about 34% for India in 2016, whereas the 2024 series puts the country at 40.1% in 2015, a gap of about 6 points (derived calculation, neighbouring but not identical years). Neither of the two is an error. In the meantime, new surveys were added and the model was rebuilt, so the past was re-estimated. If you put “India 49.4%” (2022) next to “United States 40%” (2016), you are comparing two years and two vintages of estimate: that is not a ranking, it is a mixture.

This is probably the most frequent reason why a country table circulating on the internet is wrong without anyone having invented anything. Each cell may be accurate at its source, and the row makes no sense.

The rule that follows is simple: two figures can be compared only if they come from the same study, the same year of publication, with the same definition and the same age standardisation. That is what we look at next.

Step 3 of 6 · The big groups

With equal methods, comparisons exist: by region and by sex

When the figures come from a single study, they are comparable with one another. The 2024 study, published in The Lancet Global Health, estimated prevalence for 2022 with a single model, the same definition and age standardisation.1 The WHO drew four regional figures from it.2

In 2022, high-income Asia Pacific is the least active group, and Oceania the most active

Adults aged 18 and over, 2022, age-standardised, self-reported. Source: Strain et al., Lancet Global Health, 2024; WHO press release of 26 June 2024. The press release gives only these four regional values.1,2

What this means

The result is counter-intuitive: the most inactive group is high-income Asia Pacific, and wealth alone does not sort regions. The “high-income Western countries” group, at 28%, sits below the world average of 31.3%. France belongs to it in principle, but the press release does not say so and the value specific to France is not in the pages read: this assignment is a deduction, not a figure. A group average says nothing about a country within the group.

Another gap is solid because it is measured within a single study: women are more often insufficiently active than men, 33.8% against 28.7% in 2022, about 5 points worldwide. According to the WHO, the gap reaches 20 points in some countries.1,2 In those countries, the gap between men and women is therefore well above the 3-point gap between the world average (31.3%) and the group of Western countries (28%), derived calculation.

The trend adds to the picture. Insufficient activity rose in 103 of the 197 countries and territories (52%), and in 6 of the 9 regions. Among people aged 60 and over, it rose in all regions and for both sexes.1 Worldwide, it goes from 23.4% in 2000 to 26.4% in 2010, then 31.3% in 2022.1 If this trend continues, the WHO projects 35% in 2030.2 We now know what can be compared on a world scale. But France is in Europe, where another survey asks another question, and the ranking changes.

Step 4 of 6 · Europe

Another question gives another ranking: how often people take part

Special Eurobarometer 525 on sport and physical activity, published in September 2022, surveys 26,580 Europeans across the 27 countries of the Union.8 It does not ask whether you reach 150 minutes: it asks how often you do sport or exercise. Across the Union as a whole, 38% do so at least once a week, 17% less often, and as many as 45% never.7,8

In the European Union, the range runs from 71% weekly participation in Finland to 73% “never” in Portugal

Share of people surveyed. This is not the same definition as the WHO’s 150 minutes: it is the reported frequency of doing sport or exercise. Source: Special Eurobarometer 525, 2022 (summary report).7,8

What this means

This chart does not measure the same thing as the previous one, and you cannot put Finland at 71% next to a country at 28% inactivity: one is about the frequency of sport, the other about cumulated minutes of activity in all contexts. What this second ranking shows is that the ranking depends on the question asked. The Nordic countries, the Benelux countries and Slovenia come out on top; Portugal overtook Malta as the least active country.9

France appears neither at the top nor at the bottom of the extracts read. An academic analysis of the Eurobarometer, whose abstract does not specify which wave was used, places it among the high-activity countries, together with Belgium, Germany, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, the United Kingdom and Slovenia, and places Italy, Poland, Portugal, Romania and Hungary among those with low activity.11 This is a grouping, not a percentage, and it holds for the question asked in this survey.

Even within the Eurobarometer series, the measure changes with the question: between 2017 and 2022, the share of people who take part “regularly” in a sports setting fell from 40% to 38%, whereas the share who do other physical activity rose from 44% to 50%.9 Two neighbouring questions, two opposite trends. It remains to see what happens when the indicator is no longer a report of activity, but an indirect clue.

Step 5 of 6 · The objections

Proxy indicators and self-report distort the comparison

The fifth step deals with two serious objections. The first: if the questionnaires differ, why not use more “objective” figures, such as the number of people with a gym membership? The second: what is a self-report really worth?

For the first, the 2022 Eurobarometer also gives the share of respondents with a gym or fitness club membership. It is 35% in Sweden, 29% in the Netherlands, 26% in Denmark, 13% in Germany and Spain, 11% in Italy, 9% in Poland, 6% in France and Romania, 2% in Lithuania.10

France has 6% of gym members, which says little about what the French do

Share of respondents with a gym or fitness club membership, 2022. Source: Eurobarometer 2022, as reported by Herman Rutgers (21 October 2022). Selection of countries reported by the article, not all 27.10

What this means

A membership measures consumption of services, not activity. You can walk, run, cycle or garden without a membership, and be a member without going. What this chart proves is that a proxy indicator produces a ranking that looks like none of the others: take it as a warning, not as a fitness league table.

For the second objection, the limit is acknowledged by the authors themselves. In the French analysis of adult physical activity (Esteban survey, 2014-2016), the researchers write that a questionnaire cannot objectively measure energy expenditure, that it probably overestimates light activities coded as moderate, and that objective tools such as accelerometers would be needed. They add that domestic activities are coded differently from one study to another, which makes their results not directly comparable with those of international studies.14 The World Obesity Federation country factsheet, which draws on WHO data, states for its part that the survey type is “self-reported”.15

Another French indicator shows the same risk: more than 80% of adults, men and women alike, spend more than three hours a day in front of a screen outside work (80.5% and 79.8%). The authors use it as an indicator of sedentary behaviour, and specify that it covers only part of sitting time.14

We need to be clear about what this implies. It does not make the studies useless: a reporting error may be roughly the same from one year to the next within a single country and with the same questionnaire, and it is within that frame that trends can be read. It does, however, forbid reading a gap of a few points between two countries as a difference in behaviour. There remains a solid ground, narrower than the world but more useful for you: France compared with itself.

Step 6 of 6 · The specific case

What remains comparable: France within itself

The last step is the most precise. Within a single survey, with the same questionnaire and the same population, the gaps between groups can be interpreted. For France, the national Esteban survey by Santé publique France (2014-2016) interviews adults in metropolitan France with the RPAQ questionnaire.12,13 It reports that 71% of men and 53% of women meet the WHO recommendations.12

Within a single survey, age and sex clearly separate the groups

Left: metropolitan France, Esteban 2014-2016, adults meeting the WHO recommendations according to the questionnaire.12 Right: European Union, Eurobarometer 2022, share of people doing sport regularly.8 The two panels cannot be compared with each other: different definitions and populations.

What this means

Within the French survey, a gap of 18 points separates men from women (71 against 53, derived calculation). Within the Eurobarometer, 54% of 15-24 year olds take part regularly, against 21% of those aged 55 and over: a ratio of about 2.6 (derived calculation). These gaps are measured without changing method, which makes them interpretable. For you, this is what matters: your group, your age, your sex.

The French trend is more nuanced. Since the previous survey of 2006-2007, activity has fallen among all women and risen among men aged 40 to 54; the analysis gives no figures for the other groups.12 As for children, about one boy in two and one girl in three meet the recommendations, with no change since 2006.12

What remains uncertain is important. The French data cited date from 2014-2016, before the 2020 lockdown, which may have changed habits, as the authors point out.14 They do not allow us to say where France stands in the 2022 world ranking. The WHO does publish a value for France in 2022, as for every country, but it does not appear in the pages we were able to read, and we do not reconstruct it. To read it, you have to open the WHO database, not a table reproduced on a website.

The answer to the problem

The question was twofold: where does France stand, and what can be compared. The most honest answer is this: from what we were able to read, no reliable rank can be given to France, and most of the country rankings in circulation are not comparable.

What is solid. Country figures are estimates built from self-reports, with questionnaires that differ from one country to another. The same estimate can change when the study is redone: India is at 34% for 2016 in the 2018 study, and at about 40% for 2015 in the 2024 series. Comparisons are valid when they come from the same study, the same year and the same definition: on that basis, the “high-income Western countries” region is at 28%, below the world average of 31.3%, and women are more often insufficiently active than men.

What is probable. France falls among the countries with relatively high sports participation according to the Eurobarometer (academic grouping, wave not specified), and in the group of high-income Western countries, whose average is below the world average. These are indications of general position, not a rank.

What is not established. That one country “moves more” than another at a gap of a few points; that a 2016 figure and a 2022 figure can be lined up; that an indicator such as gym memberships tells us about actual fitness; and the exact value for France in the 2022 series, which we did not read.

What to put in place

If countries cannot be compared well, what is left that is useful? Three things, in this order.

  1. Compare yourself with a simple benchmark, not a ranking.The WHO benchmark is 150 minutes of moderate activity per week, or 75 minutes of vigorous activity, or an equivalent combination.2 Write down an ordinary week, without embellishing it: it is a self-report, with the same limits as those in this article, but it gives you a starting point.
  2. Measure your fitness rather than guess it.A physical test is a measurement, not a self-report. The test on the page is designed for this: it gives you a measured result. Where a norm table by age and sex exists, it is the most solid comparison group, since that is where gaps can be read without changing method. Do it under the same conditions each time (same time of day, same warm-up, same surface).
  3. Retest at regular intervals and compare yourself with yourself.An interval of two to three months is a practical choice, not a figure from a study: long enough for a change in training to show, short enough that you do not lose the thread. The most reliable comparison you can make is the one between your score today and the one from three months ago.

One last point, which comes from the French survey: people who take part in a greater variety of leisure activities more often meet the recommendations, according to the authors, with no precise figure in the pages read.13 Varying your activities is therefore a reasonable avenue, not a proven rule. If you have chest pain, unusual breathlessness or a chronic illness, seek medical advice before increasing the intensity.

What these figures do not say
  • All country figures are self-reported and brought to a common definition by modelling; none is a measurement of activity made with a device.1,14
  • The 2016 values (Kuwait, Brazil, United States, United Kingdom, India, China, Uganda) come from secondary sources for the 2018 study, not from the article itself.5,6
  • The Eurobarometer does not measure the WHO’s 150 minutes; its country-by-country results were read only in summary reports, never in the full report, and the value for France does not appear in the extracts read.
  • The Esteban survey dates from 2014-2016 and covers metropolitan France; the 2020 lockdown came afterwards.14
  • This work describes a situation, not a cause: it does not say why a country reports more or less activity.
  • In the sources read, we found no between-country comparison of adult fitness measured in the field. This does not prove that none exists.

Frequently asked questions

Is France a good or a bad pupil?

The sources read do not allow a verdict. It belongs to a group of high-income Western countries whose average inactivity is below the world average (28% against 31.3%), and it falls among the countries with fairly high sports participation in an analysis of the Eurobarometer. Neither of these benchmarks gives a rank.1,2,11

Why do the figures for the same country change from one site to another?

Because they come from different studies, years or definitions, or from an old vintage of estimate. India is the example: about 34% for 2016 in the 2018 study, about 40% for 2015 and 49.4% for 2022 in the 2024 series.3,5

Is a questionnaire enough to know whether I move enough?

It is a starting point. The authors of the French survey consider that a questionnaire probably overestimates some light activities, and they recommend objective tools.14

Why not rank countries by fitness rather than by reported activity?

In the sources read for this article, we found no between-country comparison of adult fitness measured in the field. We therefore cannot draw a ranking from them.

What to take from this

A country ranking is a convenient way of presenting figures that were not produced to be lined up. What is comparable is the same country in the same study, the big groups within a single estimate, and above all yourself from one test to the next. For France, the exact position in the world remains to be read in the WHO database; what is certain is that a gap of a few points with another country says nothing precise about people’s fitness.
